classification_signals: This thesis consists of one case-study, two laboratory studies (Chapters 4, 5 and 6, respectively) (p. 7)
The thesis started with a case study (Chapter 4) to identify and explore all acoustical and environmental stimuli that have the potential to influence emotional responses. (p. 2)

The second and third studies (Chapters 5 and 6, respectively) further examined the stimuli that were found to have a significant influence on emotional responses in the initial case study in the laboratory setting. (p. 2)
Data were collected through the Profile of Mood States (POMS) and analysed statistically. (p. 9)
The questionnaire in the following thesis studies consisted of a quantitative section (self-rating scales) and a qualitative section (open questions). (p. 57)

limitations: The on-site condition cannot be completely controlled, leading to potential biases in results (p. 6).
The three-dimensional model of PCM only explains emotions as a combination of only the three dimensions, failing to define distinctive emotions (p. 3).
Facial expressions and physiological changes are insufficient for distinguishing emotions beyond obvious types (p. 28).
Soundscape methods often ignore implicit emotional reactions (p. 29).
The case study's participant screening criteria resulted in un-randomised samples, affecting generalisation (p. 80).
The POMS questionnaire's vigour mood state was scattered across components, making results derived from it unreliable (p. 122).
The physical setting of the laboratory environment could significantly affect mood states (p. 176).
Sound clips were designed with combinations of sound types, limiting investigation of individual sound types (p. 176).
Only a single source was recorded for each sound type, while different sound sources within a category may have different effects (p. 176).
The study only tested a particular type of music (fast tempo popular music), limiting generalisation to other music types (p. 226, 265).
The POMS questionnaire's 'tension' category should be interpreted with a caveat, and 'confusion' was not reasonable to interpret as a mood state (p. 184).
The validity of implementing appraisal theory may require further exploration (p. 278).
More emotional categories and soundscape factors should be examined for a complete understanding of human-environment relationships (p. 278).

Uncertainty remains regarding cognitive resource as a psychophysiological function, its recovery, individual differences, and how different dimensions (eventfulness, qualitative nature, appropriateness) dominate its requirement (p. 279).
The distraction effect in more complex acoustic environments is unclear (p. 280).
minimum_safe_summary: This thesis investigates the effect of urban soundscapes on emotional responses through one on-site case study and two laboratory experiments. It integrates appraisal theory to systematically understand how sound types (street music, fountain, traffic), environmental contexts (weather, visual cues, non-urban settings), and gender influence six mood states (anger, confusion, depression, fatigue, tension, vigour). Key findings indicate that live street music reduces negative moods, while shop music increases tension. Traffic and high flow-rate fountain sounds often increase negative moods and cognitive resource demands, especially in laboratory settings where they are perceived as less appropriate or more eventful. Conversely, natural or religious contexts can mitigate these negative effects, often by distracting attention or providing a more appropriate setting. Gender differences show females are generally more resilient to negative emotions but can become more susceptible beyond a certain threshold. Limitations include the controlled nature of lab studies, the specific music and sound types tested, and the need for further exploration into cognitive resource dynamics and a wider range of emotional categories.
